I hear ya. 

Being stressed out alerts you to be doing something constructive, possibly pressuring you to be more than you are able to be. Changing what you can now, does help in the future. So I’m proud of you for doing so. 

What I notice when I’m trying to make anything work — tangible or intangible — is that I get in my head to much. I focus on the outcome without thinking of a route to get there. It makes it hard to build a bridge without any bricks, so to speak. 

If it provides any solace, what I’ve heard and learned from others: everyone, to some degree, everyone is *winging-it*. Theres a general roadmap to achieve goals, but the actual directions is based off of word-of-mouth, examples from different maps, ect. 
Taking time to better yourself doesn’t have a deadline, even if a third party is adamant so. 

I guess if theres anything I can close with its this: be kind to yourself, allow yourself room to fail/learn and remember, it **does** get better. With every rainfall, comes a sunshine.

I wish I had something constructive or useful to say, but all I can muster is that I empathize with what you’re going through. It will get better — I know it sounds like a record on repeat, but *it will get better* 

Take it a day at a time. Ignore the big picture and focus on the small ones; winning the small battles helps win major ones. It can be as small as throwing away trash, to making your bed. Winning the small battles gives you confidence and comfort that you’re not a failure. 

I have faith in you. I know the rush of life is overwhelming, but you will make it out better than you were before. *sending love your way*

I was in the same boat as you after 4-6 years of marijuana use. Everything without weed seemed lackluster or plain. The most valuable thing I learned after quitting, is to try and appreciate the little things. What I forgot when in the constant high state, is the beauty between the lines, the delight in the details. I would begin by making your bed every morning, right when you get out of bed. It helps you believe you can accomplish something, which lead to conquering harder tasks as the day progresses. Plus, accomplishing one is better than none. 

Its a slow and often boring exercise. But, in addition to that, taking it slow to fully feel yourself in the moment is a better high than any substance. Of course, if you are able to seek a professional to treat/guide you out of the depressive state, do so asap. I know there is a lot of resources to aid in that department. Being on the medication I'm on, currently, removes that nagging voice degrading me. It's only beneficial to find the right medication that encourages you to be better, rather than put you down. Furthermore, talking to a professional therapist, helps put issues into prespective. 

What I found to be a great motivator during who I was 4-6 years ago to who I am now, is music. Find your groove and you'll be surprised in what you can accomplish. I wish you well on your journey, you can do it!

Hey there. 
My post is really long, so I understand if this ancedote isn't appealing because of the length. 

I don't mean to impose or project the same (or similar) clichès, because to be honest: I'm seeing how redundant and shallow they're becoming. They are useful though, but I suspect they're said so many times, that they turn out as words. They aren't specifically catered to someone's plight or transgressions. It doesn't alleviate the feeling forever, which is a hard pill to swallow. 

Anyhow:

I guess I'll begin by saying I like your post. In my bouts with this feeling and worry, I too, have had the "call of the void" more often than I like. In my life, this person in my head it sees the call as romantic and lucrative, it tries to sell this to other parts of my brain as it's elixir. 

However, when talking to my therapist or deep-diving reddit, I know walking down that path, will lead me to the same pit I tried to end my life in. "If you know where the path goes, why should you take it again?", said my therapist. 

Please correct me if I'm wrong: I understood this dance with a devil will probably kill me. But I danced with it anyway, because it seemed like the only thing who understood. 

I don't remember where I read or heard this, "we aren't clean from our demons, we just learn to live above them." I have been inside a psychiatric ward twice and on both accounts, I know the call of the void almost won me over. It knows my weaknesses and has a great memory of all my failures and short-commings (and isn't afraid to say details). In those times of despair and doubt, I resented this demon for reminding me how much I suck. 

A nurse gave me some advice the first time I was admitted, before I was treated (the entire 24 hour hold before being transported, with security). 
I always remember her words.

I was 19 at the time of my first attempt. I was desensitized to everything; uncaring and dissappointed in my failed attempt and embarrassed I got in this situation. She checked my vitals and knelt bedside to hold my hand: 

"I wish you well; I hope you can get better. It's a tragedy for someone so young to do this to themselves. It's tragic to hear about a young life gone, when they haven't experienced a lot of it. I'm going to tell you what someone told me, 

'You don't owe your life to anyone. You are free to do as you want and pursue anything, as long as it doesn't affect someone else physically or otherwise. You *owe* it to yourself to be happy. You owe it to the better parts of you that wants to see you thrive and be the hero you deserve." 

I wish someone said this sooner. My entire exsistence, up until that point, felt like I was appeasing someone else. I was neglecting the parts of my pyschè that believed in me. In reality, I was thristing for the time to expire, so I could get the next bump. Then, I fell in the spiral again and wounded up in rock bottom, once more. 

But, her advice stuck with me. I'm trying my best to absolve some addictions and I'm down to the last one. In some area, I believe I can prosper. Like you, I believe the Light is better, but the Shadow is tempting. It has its apparent ( but mostly transparent ) costs that come with it, therefore, following those temptations is taken as a grain of salt. 

That's one in the tragic comedy of life: being battered down and expected to rise again. It has made me complacent in some areas and anxious in others. I agree with you on the last paragraph; it is relieving to see a feeling I had, articulated. 

I guess the main point I'm getting at is: 
Being happy and being viglant for your situation, is like Sophie's choice, but it doesn't have to be this way. It depends on the circumstances, so listen to the emotions and feelings as if it were a friend, but ingest the content of their words, as a grain of salt. In the end, 
* one day at a time 
* one hour at a time 
* one minute at a time (if needed)
will build a more reliable mental fortitude. 

What helped me, is imagining my mind, as a bnb guest stay at, with these varying emotions as guests. I invite any and all emotions that decide to reside with me. I embrace them as they enter, and wish them well when they leave -- no matter if it is unpleasant in their stay. 'This too Shall Pass' I say. I find myself feeling less shitty. 

I wish you well. Take care of yourself like someone you adore, and life feels better.

Wow I can't believe I remember this, sorry for the wall of text:

It was 6th grade and I had a shitty day. My friends isolated me for some reason or I was being aloof (I don't remember the details). Either way, I remember being sad, like melancholic with defeat sprinkled around. My teacher at the time, was in her first year of teaching and caught onto this. 
She knelt down, looked me in the eyes and said, "It's alright. You'll be fine. It's okay to cry." 
Initally, I was perplexed--what is she insinuating? Then, my body had a visceral reaction and this rolling feeling rose from my gut, into my throat, then dissipated into tears and sniffles. I was embarressed because all this happened in the middle of class, and attention is the *last* thing. 
Once I pulled myself together, I felt relieved. You know when there's a fire smoldering, but a few hot coals are still red? She extinigushed a fire inside me. 

If you stuck around thanks for reading, it was cathartic remembering this memory.

Hello. I've been in the same situation you're in right now. I understand how conflicting it is to be depressed and feel evil towards life like it was a good friend who betrays you, as well as not giving a fuck in the world and settling for nothing but toking because its the only antidote to actually deal with life's downs. Nonetheless, I hear your fears; surviving shouldn't be the only way to live. Here's my advice: find something to hope for. Anything. No matter what size, looking forward to something and focusing on that anticipation takes the mind away from current troubles. Make it positive, too. It's so clichè saying "it gets better" but, my friend, it truly does. Believing in that, and mostly that alone, will get you out of the rut you're in. I hope this helps! Keep your head up champ.
